planting.note: Divide and transplant crowns in early spring or fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; established plants tolerate wetter sites than most Dryopteris.

directions: This tall, robust woodland fern of northeastern swamps and wet forests is one of the largest native Dryopteris, arising from a stout, slowly creeping crown. Plant in consistently moist to wet, richly organic soil in a shaded site such as a streamside bed or bog garden edge, mimicking the calcareous wet woods where it naturally occurs. It tolerates standing water better than most wood ferns but also grows well in ordinary moist shade borders. Clumps expand gradually and rarely need division except to propagate; simply separate rooted crown sections in spring.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society (Native Plant Trust) Go Botany

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions in fall into humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil; seed needs a cold, moist stratification period and germinates erratically, so division or purchased plugs are far more reliable.

directions: Native to Pacific Northwest forests, this low rosette-forming perennial produces rounded, scalloped leaves and short spikes of pale lavender-blue flowers among the very first blooms of the woodland year, often opening while snow still lingers. Grow in dappled to full shade under deciduous trees in soil that stays moist through spring but can dry somewhat once the canopy leafs out, matching its natural summer-dormant cycle. It slowly forms an evergreen-leaved groundcover patch and pairs well with trillium and fawn lily in a Pacific woodland garden. Leave foliage undisturbed through summer even as it fades, since the plant is simply going dormant rather than declining.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall under deep shade in acidic, humus-rich soil that stays moist year-round, as in a coastal redwood or Douglas-fir understory planting.

directions: Endemic to redwood and mixed-conifer forests of coastal California and Oregon, this rhizomatous perennial forms a rosette of broad, glossy leaves topped by clusters of rose-pink to magenta bell-shaped flowers in late spring, followed by showy deep-blue berries. It needs cool, consistently moist, acidic duff and heavy shade to thrive, making it a good companion for redwood sorrel and western sword fern in a Pacific Coast woodland garden. Growth and spread are slow, so allow several years for clumps to establish before dividing. Avoid drying out the root zone, since this species does not tolerate summer drought the way inland Clintonia species can.

planting.note: Only plant nursery-propagated stock (never wild-collected) into rich, well-drained deciduous woodland soil in fall; this species relies on specific soil mycorrhizae and resents transplanting once established.

directions: One of the easiest native terrestrial orchids to grow given the right site, this species sends up a pair of broad basal leaves and a short spike of pink-and-white or lavender-and-white hooded flowers in mid-spring. It requires rich, calcium-rich, well-drained soil in deep deciduous shade with a stable population of native soil fungi, so it establishes best when planted near existing woodland plants rather than in isolated garden beds. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants from reputable native plant specialists, since wild populations are slow to recover from collection. Once settled, clumps slowly increase by offsets and can persist for decades undisturbed.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall, 3-4 inches deep, into rich, well-drained deciduous woodland soil; this sterile double-flowered form must be propagated by division and never sets viable seed.

directions: This long-cultivated heirloom selection of the classic white wakerobin produces fully double, camellia-like white flowers instead of the species' simple three-petaled bloom, lasting notably longer in the garden since the flowers are sterile and never fade to pink or set seed. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil under deciduous trees, exactly as for the wild species, and be patient, since rhizomes are slow to bulk up and division is the only means of increase. It is considerably more expensive and slower to establish than seed-grown Trillium grandiflorum, so start with the largest rhizome available and avoid disturbing it once planted. Mulch with leaf litter annually to replicate its native forest floor habitat.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Powder Blue Giant Dwarf Crested Iris

planting.note: Plant shallow rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil; this cultivar spreads faster and blooms nearly twice the size of the wild species.

directions: Discovered by Samuel Norris in a Kentucky roadbank colony and later named and registered by Joe Pye Weed's Garden, this selection carries flowers nearly twice the size of typical dwarf crested iris — a full 3 inches across — in soft powder-blue with gold crests and deep-blue accents on the falls. Plant shallow rhizomes in humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to moderate shade, where it forms a dense, fast-spreading carpet of fan-shaped leaves ideal for edging shaded paths or covering slopes under deciduous trees. Established colonies bloom heavily for two to three weeks in mid-spring before the tree canopy fully leafs out, then remain as attractive dense foliage through summer. Divide congested clumps after flowering if bloom declines, replanting divisions immediately since rhizomes dry out quickly if exposed.
